client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. Before we dive in, I just want to check in — how are you coming in today compared to when we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly... not great. I had a really rough week. And then the lab results came back and my doctor called me, and it just — it kind of freaked me out more than I expected it to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hearing it from your doctor made it land differently — more real than it had been before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. She said my liver enzymes were elevated. She wasn't panicking or anything, but she said I should — quote — think about my alcohol intake. And I don't know, hearing it out loud from an actual doctor just... it wasn't something I could brush off. Like I've been doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned last session you were hoping to cut back this week. What ended up happening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I tried. I really did. Monday and Tuesday I stopped at one glass, which felt like — okay, that's something. But then Wednesday the baby was up basically the whole night, and my husband had to leave early, and I just... I ended up finishing the whole bottle. And then Thursday I did the same thing. So yeah. Kind of back to square one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You actually did something you set out to do for two days — and then a really brutal night knocked you sideways.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's so frustrating because I'm not — I'm not naive about it, you know? I know finishing a bottle is too much. But in that moment it feels like the only relief I get. It's the only quiet part of my entire day and I just... I can't seem to choose anything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made real progress Monday and Tuesday. And right now, even after a hard week, you're sitting here being completely honest with yourself about what happened. That kind of honesty is actually not easy — it takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. It doesn't feel like much when Wednesday happened. Like, what's the point of two good days if I just collapse the second things get hard?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear that frustration. Can I ask — when you imagine why you want this to actually be different, what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Maeve. My daughter. I keep thinking about what it would feel like when she's old enough to notice. Like I don't want her to have this memory of me being a little off every night. My mom was like that and I swore I would never —

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You carry this picture of the mother you want to be for Maeve. And it matters deeply to you that she gets something different from what you had growing up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. I love her so much it's almost scary, like the feeling is so big. And the drinking is just — it's the opposite of everything I want. I don't know how I got so stuck in this without even really noticing it happening.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this gap — between who you're being in those evenings and who you want to be for her. What do you think is underneath the pattern, beyond just the stress of the hard days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I never actually dealt with the postpartum stuff. I kept telling myself I was fine, just push through. And the wine became like a signal that the hard part of the day was over, even though technically the hard part never ends with a newborn. I think I've been using it to feel like myself again. Because I don't actually know how to feel like myself anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, see if I've got it right. You came in today shaken by those lab results — that was a real wake-up call. You actually did cut back early in the week, which matters, and then a brutal night pulled you off course. You're not in denial about what's happening — you see it clearly. And underneath all of it is this love for Maeve and a real fear that the drinking is moving you away from the mother you want to be for her. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — when you lay it out like that, it doesn't feel like I'm just broken or whatever. It feels like there's an actual reason this started and maybe... I don't know, maybe an actual way through it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would a first step look like to you — something small and real, not perfect?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not buying the second bottle when the first one's gone. Right now I always have two in the fridge, like by default. If there's only one, at least there's a ceiling. And maybe texting my husband when I feel myself getting overwhelmed instead of waiting until I'm already in the kitchen reaching for it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just came up with two really concrete strategies on your own — reducing access before the moment hits, and pulling in support before you're already in the crisis point. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It sounds almost too simple when I say it out loud. But I think simple might be what I can actually do right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Would it be okay if I shared something that might be useful here? A lot of people find that the urge to drink peaks in a pretty short window — maybe twenty, thirty minutes — and if you can get through that window doing something else, it often passes on its own. It's not about willpower holding forever, just bridging that one moment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That actually makes a lot of sense. Because it does feel like a wave kind of thing. Like if I could just — put Maeve in the carrier and walk around the block, by the time I got back maybe the worst of it would be past. And she loves being in the carrier so it's not even — it's something good for both of us.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've got the one-bottle limit, texting your husband, and the carrier walk. Which of those feels most doable to actually try first this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The walk, honestly. Because it gets me out of the kitchen — which is kind of the danger zone — and it's also just... it's something I'm doing with her. Not instead of her. That feels right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to close by saying what I see. You came in today anxious, after a hard week and some scary news from your doctor. And you've moved somewhere very different by the end of this hour. You connected this to what matters most — Maeve — and you built a concrete, realistic plan that fits your actual life. The lab results were a jolt, and instead of shutting down, you turned toward it. That's significant work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I needed to hear that. I'm still scared, but it feels different now. Less like panicking and more like... okay, I can actually do something with this.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey. Come on in, take a seat wherever feels comfortable. I'm glad you're here. There's no rush — we can just take a breath for a second.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Uh... okay. I don't really — I mean, they kind of told me I should come here. From the ER. I've never done this before, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that like — being in the ER last night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Unnecessary. I had a few drinks, I fell, it wasn't — I mean people are acting like it's some huge thing. It's not. I'm fine. My wife freaked out and called 911, that's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're fine... and at the same time, you're sitting here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. She made me come. Look, I don't have a problem. In the military — that's just what you do, man. Every deployment, every homecoming, you drink. You decompress. It's not like... it's not a disease or whatever they put on the pamphlets.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking was part of the culture, part of how you and the guys got through it. What was it getting you through?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... you see things over there. You need to shut your brain off. And when you come home it doesn't — your brain doesn't just stop. So. [pause] It works. That's all I'm saying. It works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You carried things home from deployment that most people never have to carry. And you found something that helped you survive that. That took real grit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. [long pause] Yeah, it did. It does. I'm not gonna pretend. But now she's saying she'll leave if I don't get — if I don't get help. [pause] I don't even know what that means. Get help. Like this is gonna fix whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The person you love most is telling you she might go. That's landing differently than anything else has.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's done it before. Threatened. So I don't know if she means it this time. But... [long pause] ...she had her bags out. Like, actual bags. In the hallway. And my daughter was standing there crying. She's seven. She shouldn't — she shouldn't have to see that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was going through your mind when you saw those bags?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought... okay, this is it. And then I just went blank. Which is what I always do. [pause] I go blank and I pour a drink and I — [trails off] My daughter. The way she looked at me, man. I can't — I don't know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Like she needed you to show up differently.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [quietly] Yeah. She's seven. She just wants her dad, you know? And I'm... I don't know what I am anymore. I came back from deployment thinking — okay, now I just get to be home. Be normal. But it's not like that. It's not like that at all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would being the dad she needs — what would that even look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd be... present. Like actually present, not just in the room. Not just staring at the TV with a beer. [pause] I remember my own dad. He was checked out. His whole life. And I swore — I literally swore to myself I wouldn't be that guy. [pause] And here I am being that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made a promise to yourself a long time ago about the kind of father you'd be. And it still matters to you. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't talked about my dad in... [pause] I don't know why I said that. [pause] Maybe because I'm scared I'm already him and I just — I didn't let myself see it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I can reflect back what I'm hearing, make sure I'm getting it right. You came in not sure you needed to be here. In your world — the military, what you lived through — drinking made sense, it helped you get through things that were genuinely hard. But something shifted when you saw those bags, when you saw your daughter's face. And underneath all of it, there's this fear that you might be becoming someone you promised yourself you'd never be. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [pause] Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I didn't expect someone to just say it like that. Out loud. [exhale] It sounds different hearing it back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things were actually different six months from now — if something had changed — what would that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd still be married. [small laugh] That's the first thing. And my daughter — she'd run to me when I got home. She still does it now but... I can see it. She's starting to check the room first when she walks in. See what kind of mood I'm in. Kids shouldn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's already learned to read the room. And you don't want her to have to do that anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. God, no. [pause] I didn't realize I was doing that to her. I thought I was keeping it together. But she knows, doesn't she. Kids always know. [pause] That's — yeah. That's not okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today not knowing what to expect, maybe not sure you had anything to talk about. And somewhere in this hour you started talking about what you actually want — to be present for your daughter, to not lose your wife, to not repeat what you grew up in. Those are yours. I'm not going to tell you what to do with them. But I hope you'll come back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] Yeah. I don't have everything figured out, I'm not saying that. But. [pause] Yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab a seat wherever's comfortable. So, Dr. Martinez referred you over, and I just want to be upfront with you from the jump: I'm not here to lecture you or tell you what to do. I'm just curious about what's going on in your life. What would you say brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor brought me here. That's what brought me here. Look, I'm going to be honest with you — I don't think I have a problem. I've got two kids, no help from anyone, a full-time job, and apparently now I have to come in and explain myself because I have a glass of wine at night. I mean. That's just not fair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this really wasn't your idea — and that makes complete sense. Coming in to talk to a stranger about your personal life isn't most people's first choice on a Tuesday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No offense, but no. It's really not. I'm not some — I'm not a person with a drinking problem, okay? My kids are fed. The house is clean. I don't miss work. I just have wine to wind down. Maybe a little more on bad nights. But who doesn't? Seriously, who doesn't?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The kids are taken care of, work is fine, house is clean — you're holding everything together. What does a typical evening look like once the kids are finally in bed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It looks like finally sitting down for the first time all day. I do dinner, homework, bath time, bedtime — all of it, alone. And then... yeah. I pour a glass of wine and I watch something. And I just breathe. That's my time. That's literally the only thing in my entire day that's mine, and now apparently that's a problem too.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying all of that every single day. By yourself. That's genuinely not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Don't — don't do that. Don't feel sorry for me. I didn't come here for that. I'm fine. We're managing. I just don't need someone picking apart my evenings like I'm some kind of... I don't know. Just don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough — no pity, I'll put that away. You mentioned 'a little more on bad nights.' What does a bad night actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... a bottle. Maybe. I don't — it's not every night. But when there's a call from school, or my ex is late on money again, or my youngest has a full meltdown at eight PM, I just... I need something to take the edge off. Wine is legal. I'm not out here doing anything crazy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: On those nights — the call from school, the money stress, the meltdown — the wine is the one thing that doesn't need anything from you. Doesn't judge, doesn't ask.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. Everything else is just... loud. All the time. And it makes things quiet for a little while. Is that really so wrong?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it feel like right before you pour that first glass — like, what's going on in your body, your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like I'm... depleted. Like I'm running on nothing and everything still wants more from me. And kind of angry, I guess. Not at anyone specific. Just — why is it always all on me? Every single day. Why is it always all on me?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That anger — that 'why is this all on me' — that sounds like it's been sitting in your chest for a really long time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It has. Yeah. And I know — I know the wine isn't actually fixing any of it. I'm not delusional. But it's the only thing that gives me any real relief and I don't... I've never known what else to do. I've just never figured that out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Saying 'I know it's not fixing it' out loud — that takes a kind of honesty a lot of people can't quite get to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been saying it to myself for a while, so... I've also noticed — I need more now than I used to. Like, one glass doesn't even do anything anymore. And that scares me a little. I won't pretend it doesn't. That's not great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing — see if I've got it right. You're doing everything: the kids, the job, the house, alone. And every night the wine is the one moment that belongs to you, that makes things quiet. And at the same time, something in you has noticed it's shifting — you need more to get the same feeling, and that's starting to worry you. Both of those things are true at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah, that's pretty accurate. I didn't think this conversation was going to go like this. I thought you were just going to hand me a pamphlet and send me home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No pamphlets, I promise. Well — I have some. But I'll hide them. What would it look like for you, a year from now, if nothing changed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want that. I think about my mom a lot. She drank. It was... worse than me, I think, but. I swore I was never going to be her. And sometimes I wonder if I'm heading there. I don't want my kids to see me that way. I can't be that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your kids. Not becoming your mom. That's a really important line for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. It really is. She got bad. And I love my kids more than anything. I just — I genuinely don't know how to get through the evenings without it. Like, what am I supposed to do instead? Just... sit there with all of it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That is actually exactly the right question. What else could help you exhale at the end of the day — actually exhale — that isn't the wine? Even if it sounds small or kind of dumb.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I honestly don't know. I've never thought about it that way. Like, treating the exhaustion as its own thing instead of just — numbing how I feel about it. Maybe that's the part I've been getting wrong this whole time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today not wanting to be here at all, and you just figured something out that some people spend years circling around without seeing. I don't want to pile too much on in one session — but there's real stuff here worth talking about: the exhaustion, what support could actually look like, what you want your nights to feel like. If you're open to coming back, I think we can do something with this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah, okay. I'm not promising I'm going to like it. But yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. ... I want you to know — that means something. Especially after the week you've had.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My mom literally drove me here and waited outside. So. Yeah. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't really choose to be here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — no. Not really. I don't see why any of this is necessary. I went to the hospital, I'm fine, I came home. Done. But now it's like, everyone's treating me like I'm some kind of like... addict or something. I'm eighteen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like having everyone suddenly paying this much attention to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's — ugh. It's so annoying. Like I feel like I'm being watched all the time now. My mom's checking my bag. The school has me flagged or whatever. And now you. And I just — I didn't do anything that everybody else isn't doing. Literally everyone drinks.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel singled out. Like the rules applied to you but not to everyone else doing the same thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because that's what happened! My friend Kayla drinks way more than me. She's been doing it since like sophomore year. But I end up in an ER one time and suddenly I'm the problem. It's not fair and nobody wants to hear that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you. ... Can I ask — what do you actually remember about that night? Only what you're comfortable sharing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I remember being at Jake's. There were shots going around and everyone was doing them so I just... kept up. And then it gets kind of... blurry. And then I woke up and I was in the hospital and my mom was there and she was just — she was crying. And I don't know. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Seeing your mom cry... that's stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I felt bad about that part. I do. But it was an accident. Like I didn't plan for it to go that far. It's not like I have some — some problem. I just had too much. It happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't plan for it to go that far. ... That gap — where things go blurry and then blank — what's it like sitting with that? Not knowing what happened in between?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... weird. It's kind of weird. I don't love it. Like, I know people black out, it's not some rare thing. But I don't know. I don't really know what happened to me between Jake's and the hospital and that's just... it's kind of a lot to think about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something in you doesn't fully sit easy with it. Even if you're not ready to call it scary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess. I woke up and my throat hurt and I was in a hospital gown and I didn't — I didn't know how I got there. And my mom had been there for hours apparently. So. That wasn't great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You care about your mom. And underneath all the anger at everyone making this into a bigger thing than you think it is — there's a part of you that already knows it was a bigger thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. Maybe. I just — I didn't want her to see me like that. That's the part that actually bothers me. Like not the school stuff, not you, just... her face.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Her face is what you keep coming back to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. She looked... she looked really scared. And I just kept thinking like, what did I miss. What happened that she looked that scared. And I can't answer that because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to ask you something and I want you to know there's no right answer. Not what your mom wants. Not what the school wants. What do you actually want — going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I don't know. I don't want her to look at me like that again. And I guess — I keep thinking about why I couldn't just stop. Like everyone else was doing shots and I just kept going and I don't know why I couldn't just... stop at some point. Like why can't I do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just... try to hold all of this together for a second. You didn't plan for any of this. You were keeping up with everyone else, which is something that feels really important in those moments. And then you woke up in a place you didn't expect, with your mom terrified, and a gap in your memory you can't fill. And now you're sitting here asking yourself — why couldn't I stop? That's not a small question. That's actually a really honest one.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's kind of exactly it. I've never really said it out loud like that but. Yeah. I don't know why I can't just stop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine being at a party and just... not drinking. Or stopping early. What comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... everyone looking at me. Feeling weird. Being the only one not doing it. I've tried that and it's just — it's lonely. Even when you're in a room full of people it's like you're not really there. You're just... watching. And I hate that feeling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Really being there — belonging — that matters deeply to you. ... And I wonder if part of what you're starting to see is that the drinking was supposed to close that gap. Make you feel more there. And maybe it's doing something closer to the opposite.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Maybe. I don't know. I haven't thought about it like that before. But... maybe.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know first sessions can feel a little strange — sitting down with someone you've never met and just... talking. So no pressure to have it all figured out. How are you doing right now, walking in here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, honestly a little nervous. I've never done anything like this before. I wasn't really sure what to expect, so... yeah. I'm here, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a completely normal way to feel walking through that door for the first time. What made you decide to come in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My friend basically staged this whole... I don't know, it wasn't like a full intervention or whatever, but she sat me down and was pretty serious about it. Said she was worried. And I figured — I don't know, I figured I'd at least hear what someone professional has to say. She doesn't usually get like that, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So her concern was enough to get you here. Like she saw something that made you think, maybe I should pay attention to this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... I think she was maybe overreacting a little bit. But she's known me for a long time, so. I figured it couldn't hurt to come in. I'm not like — I'm not saying I have a problem. I just wanted to see what this was about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. Tell me about your drinking — what does a typical week actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I bartend, so my schedule's pretty chaotic. Most nights I work till one, two in the morning. And yeah, I usually have some drinks after my shift to wind down. It's kind of the culture, you know? Everyone I work with does it. It's not like I'm sitting at home alone drinking by myself at noon or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's how you decompress. And it makes sense in that environment — it's what everyone around you does. So it's felt pretty normal up until... something shifted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean it did feel normal. But the other day I was just kind of sitting there and I tried to think of the last time I didn't drink. And I... couldn't. Like I genuinely tried to think back and there wasn't a day I could point to. That kind of freaked me out, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment — when you couldn't find that day — what was going through your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was just... weird. Really unsettling. Because I've always thought of myself as like a casual drinker, social drinker, whatever. But if I can't find one day — not one — then that doesn't really sound casual anymore, does it? That sounds like something different. And I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real honesty to let that question actually land instead of brushing it off. A lot of people wouldn't let themselves go there. You did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm still here, so. I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What worries you most about what you noticed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'm scared it's already further along than I think it is. Like I'm 27. I don't want to be the guy who's 45 and his whole life is just this. I've seen those bartenders. The lifers. And they're not — they don't look happy. They look stuck. And I don't want to be stuck.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're looking down the road and you don't like what you see at the end of it. And somewhere underneath that, there's a version of yourself you're trying to protect.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I just don't know how I got here this fast, you know? It kind of snuck up on me. Like I wasn't even paying attention and then all of a sudden it's just... every day. Without thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture your life looking different — less drinking, or even no drinking — what comes up for you? Does that feel like something that's even possible?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly I don't know. The job makes it really hard. Like, free drinks are literally part of the culture, and if I'm not drinking with the regulars or after a shift I'm kind of... on the outside of something. But I also think I've been using that as a reason to not look at it too closely. Maybe. I'm not sure. It's like both things are true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I'm getting it right. You came in because someone who cares about you pushed you to, but you also had your own wake-up call — that moment you couldn't name a sober day. You're not in a panic, but you're paying attention. You're looking at these older bartenders and you're worried about the road you're on. And you're starting to wonder if the job culture has been a convenient explanation for something that's actually bigger than that. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... when you say it like that it sounds really clear. I think I've been kind of avoiding putting it together like that. It's easier to just not think about it too hard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would you want to be different, if anything?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just want to know I actually have a choice. Like, I want to be able to have one drink or no drinks and be okay with that. Right now I'm... I'm not sure I could do that. And that bothers me more than anything else, I think. The fact that I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Wanting to have a real choice — that's not a small thing. That's you saying something about the kind of life you want and how you want to move through it. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never... I never thought about it like that. As like, a freedom thing. But yeah. I think that is what I'm saying. I want it to be a choice, not just a thing that happens every night because I don't know how to stop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So where does that leave you right now? What feels like a useful next step, even if it's just a small one?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I want to come back. Which — I didn't expect to say that walking in here. I thought I was just going to do this once and tell my friend I tried. But I think I actually need to figure this out. I don't want to just keep going like nothing's wrong when something... something probably is.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know that's not always easy, especially right after finishing a program. What brings you here — what made today the day you decided to walk through that door?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I read something online. An article. Look, I'm not — I don't have some massive problem. I just finished the detox thing, figured I might as well... see what this is. I don't know. My wife's been on me and I thought fine, fine, I'll go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You finished a detox program and still showed up here. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Don't do that. Don't — I run a company of four hundred people. I don't need to be... I'm not some kind of... I'm not an alcoholic. I drink. Plenty of people drink. My father drank. It's what we do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you — your sense of who you are — if the word 'alcoholic' actually fit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It doesn't fit. That's the point. I haven't missed a board meeting in six years. My numbers are good. My team respects me. Whatever I do at home at night has nothing to do with any of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your work has been solid — and yet something still got you into that detox program.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That was... that was my wife pushing for that. She thinks everything is a catastrophe. I did it to get her off my back, honestly. To show her — look, see? I can stop. Done. Happy now?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's real tension between what she sees and what you experience. She's watching something you don't think is there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She doesn't understand what my job is like. The pressure I'm under is — it's not normal pressure. The scotch helps me decompress. That's it. That's stress management, not... not whatever she thinks it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Walk me through a typical evening. What does that actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home around eight, nine usually. Pour a glass. Watch the news. Pour another. I just... it's my time, you know? I've been on since six in the morning. I've earned that. It winds me down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've earned time to yourself. And by the end of that wind-down, a bottle gets finished.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Most nights. But I wake up fine. I'm at my desk by seven, I'm sharp. Nobody who works with me sees a problem. Except — look, people who don't understand the context see a problem. That's different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'nobody who works with me sees a problem' — and then you stopped yourself mid-sentence.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I meant... my wife. And my assistant said something once. But that was one time, it was a brutal week, I'd had a drink at lunch and she — it's not a pattern. It was a rough stretch.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your assistant noticed something at work. What exactly did she say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She... she said she could smell it. In the afternoon. She was — she was very careful about how she said it, which made it worse somehow. I told her it was mouthwash. She didn't push back but... she knew.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm noticing it's getting harder to hold the line that nothing's actually wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The detox was... I didn't expect it. The shaking. I thought I'd just stop and that would be it — I've got willpower, that's never been my problem. But my hands were... and I couldn't sleep for three days. I didn't know your body could do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You expected to be in control of stopping, the same way you're in control of everything else. And then your body did something completely outside of your control.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that... that scared me. I don't say that easily. I haven't said that out loud to anyone. My wife doesn't even know how bad those three days were.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty to say — and I think part of you already knows that what scared you is trying to tell you something important.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My son is sixteen. He... he used to ask me to watch games with him on Sunday. He stopped asking. I didn't notice for a while and then I did and I... I put it together. What he was seeing on Sunday nights.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine things being different — what does that actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Being... present, I guess. Actually being there when I'm there. Not just sitting in the same room going through the motions until I can pour another drink. Actually watching the game. Remembering it the next day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know exactly what version of yourself you want to get back to. That's not a small thing — that's the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe I do. It's just... fifteen years. I don't fully know who I am without it. That sounds ridiculous coming from me. But I'm here, aren't I. That's... that's something.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Sarah — one of the counselors here. I know this probably wasn't how you were planning to spend your morning. I'm really glad you're okay physically. Can you tell me a little bit about what's going on for you right now, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm fine. The doctors already checked everything, I don't have any injuries. I honestly don't know why I'm sitting here. The nurse said I had to talk to someone before they'd discharge me, so. Here I am. I don't really know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. You didn't choose to be here today. That's a hard position to be in. What would you want me to know about what happened last night — from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What happened is that I made one stupid mistake. I went to a work dinner — which is literally part of my job — had some drinks, like everyone else there, and then drove home and got pulled over. That's it. That's the whole story. It doesn't mean I have some kind of problem. People mess up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're really clear on that. One mistake. And you don't want it to mean more than it does.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Because everyone is acting like I'm some kind of disaster. My mom called at six in the morning — six — my coworkers are going to find out about this somehow, I just know it. I'm 28. I have a career. I have an apartment, I go to the gym, I have my life together. I'm not some alcoholic sitting in a gutter somewhere. I had too much at a work event and made a bad call. It happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're already managing so much — your own feelings, your mom, worrying about work. That's a heavy morning on top of a hard night. What was the dinner actually like before everything happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was a client pitch dinner. High stakes, open bar, nice restaurant downtown. My director had been breathing down my neck about this account all week. And I was fine, I was totally holding it together — I always do. I just... I don't know, I drank more than I meant to. Maybe because I hadn't eaten much. Maybe because I was just so relieved for the dinner part to be over. But I wasn't falling down or slurring or whatever. I genuinely thought I was okay to drive.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You'd been running hard all week. High-pressure pitch, then a high-stakes night — and you thought you had it under control. And that's how it usually goes for you. You handle it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because I do handle it. I've done a hundred of those dinners. I know how to hold myself together. Last night just... something was off, I don't know. I misjudged it. But that doesn't make it a pattern. One data point isn't a pattern.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One data point isn't a pattern. And... you mentioned that maybe you drank faster because you were stressed. That word keeps staying with me. You carry a lot, and you keep showing up anyway. That takes something real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I'm stressed because work is stressful. That's just — that's life. That's everyone my age with an actual job. I'm not drinking to cope, if that's where you're going with this. God, I knew this was going to be that kind of conversation.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not going anywhere with it. I'm genuinely asking. What was actually happening for you that night before you even walked into the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was just... a lot. My director had basically implied my position on the account was on the line if the pitch didn't land. And right before I left for dinner I got like three texts from my landlord — lease going up, of course it is. I just walked in already kind of fried. I just wanted to get through it and go home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you walked into that room already depleted. Work pressure, money stress — and maybe the drinks were the first moment all night where you could just... stop bracing for something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds like a problem. It wasn't — I wasn't trying to escape or whatever. I just didn't plan to drink that much. And then my car was right there and I just didn't think. I wasn't thinking at all. I just wanted to be in my own bed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I just... reflect back what I'm hearing? You went into a really hard night already stretched thin. You drank more than you intended — maybe because some part of you needed a moment of relief. And then you made a call about your car that you're now living with the fallout from. You don't see yourself as someone with a problem. And you're also sitting in an ER at eight in the morning, and you know it could have gone a lot worse.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. It could've been a lot worse. Nobody got hurt. I know that, okay? I'm not oblivious to that. I just — I don't think that means I need to check into somewhere or blow up my entire life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nobody's saying that. I want to ask you something different. What does drinking give you — not last night specifically, just in general, in your life? What does it actually do for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... helps me unwind. After work, at events. I'm actually pretty introverted — which is kind of ironic given my job — and these client dinners are genuinely exhausting. So it takes the edge off. Makes it easier to be on. I could stop if I wanted to. I just... haven't really wanted to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It does something real for you. It makes hard things feel more manageable. And you believe you could stop — that's not a small thing to know about yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've just never had to think about it before. It's always just been there — drinks after work, drinks at events, drinks on the weekend with friends. That's just... that's being in your twenties, right? But I guess last night was the first time it actually cost me something real. And I don't want that to happen again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "I don't want that to happen again." That's real. After the night you've had — that's not a small thing to say.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've worked really hard to build my life. I moved to this city knowing literally no one. Got this job on my own. And I just... I don't want to be the person who unravels it over something stupid. That actually scares me — more than the DUI charge, I think. The idea that I could just lose what I built.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image of yourself — someone who built something real, on her own terms — that's clearly at the center of all of this. So what would protecting that actually look like for you? Not what anyone else would say. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I need to be smarter about it. Have a plan before I go somewhere, not after. Like, Uber booked before the first drink, not after the fourth. Or just don't drink at work things at all. And maybe be more honest with myself about how much I'm actually having. I'm not saying I need to quit. But... maybe I've been a little careless.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here not knowing why you were here, not sure you had anything to say. And now — without me pushing you anywhere — you're thinking about what being careful actually means for you. You're not ready to label anything, and that's completely okay. But something shifted this morning. That 'I don't want that to happen again' — that came from you. That's yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I guess it did. I still think I'm going to be okay. But maybe I don't have to have all the answers right this second. I'm just — I'm really tired. I want to go home and sleep. But... yeah. Maybe talking wasn't the worst thing.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know it can feel a little awkward walking into a new office, meeting somebody you don't know. There's no agenda here, no checklist we have to get through. I'm just curious — what's it like for you, being here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... honestly? A little weird. I've done the VA thing before, like the doctors and whatever, that's fine. But this kind of — sitting in a room talking about feelings — I don't know. My last therapist referred me here and I figured, okay, one more shot I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One more shot. That tells me something — that even with some doubt in the room, you still showed up. What happened with the last therapist, if you don't mind me asking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... stopped going. It wasn't like a big thing. She was fine, I guess. It just felt like — I don't know — like I'd say something and she'd write stuff down and then ask me how that made me feel. Every time. Just felt like going through motions. I've got enough of that in my life already.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It felt mechanical. Like you were being processed rather than actually heard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And I get it, they've got a lot of patients, it's the VA, whatever. I'm not — I'm not complaining. I just... I don't know what I'm supposed to get out of it. Out of any of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That uncertainty makes a lot of sense to me. And I want you to know, I'm not going to pretend I have all the answers for you today. I guess I'm just wondering — when you think about what brought you here, what comes up for you first?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The drinking, I guess. That's what they want to talk about. My doctor flagged it, my therapist mentioned it... everybody's got an opinion. Look, I drink. It's not — I'm not passed out in a ditch somewhere. I work, I pay my bills, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're managing. Keeping things together. And at the same time, it sounds a little frustrating — like everyone around you has decided there's a problem before you've even had a chance to define it yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Like I'm a case to be solved. I've got depression, okay, I've had it for years, and yeah, sometimes a couple beers at night is the only thing that actually lets me... I don't know, breathe. Turn the volume down. Is that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Turn the volume down. I want to stay with that image for a second, if that's okay. It sounds like there's a lot of... noise. Inside, I mean.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, there is. I don't — look, it's not like I'm sitting there happy about it. I know it's not a great solution. I'm not an idiot. But what else am I supposed to do at ten o'clock at night when my brain won't shut up?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know it's not a great solution. That's actually... that takes some honesty to say out loud. And I hear the exhaustion in it — like you've been dealing with this noise for a long time and you found something that works, at least in the short term, even if part of you isn't fully at peace with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been dealing with it since — I don't know, my late twenties? Service didn't help. Coming back didn't help. I've tried meds. Some worked for a while, then they stopped, or the side effects were... and then you're just — you're just adjusting dosages forever and it feels pointless. The drinking at least feels like I'm in control of something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Control is really important to you. After feeling like so much — the depression, the meds, maybe things from your service — after feeling like so much of that was out of your hands, having one thing you could reach for and count on... that makes sense. What does it feel like, the night after? The next morning?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Not great. If I'm honest. I'm tired. More tired than I should be. And sometimes I feel kind of — guilty, I guess? Like I know I'm not doing myself any favors. But then the day gets going and you just push through it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's a cost. The relief it gives you at night... and then the guilt in the morning, the fatigue. You push through, but it's still there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is still there. The noise doesn't actually go away, does it. It's just... postponed. And then the next night it's the same thing. I've thought about that. More than I probably let on to people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been sitting with this privately for a long time. That's a hard place to be. I'm glad you're saying it out loud today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... I'm tired of feeling like this is just how it is for me. Like this is just — my life. I don't know if I believe it can be different, but I don't want to be doing this at fifty, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a part of you that's tired of it. That doesn't want this to still be the story at fifty. Even if you're not sure it can change — that part of you showed up today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think that's... that's actually why I came. Not because Dr. Reyes told me to — well, partly — but I've been thinking lately, like, what would it even feel like to have a quiet night without needing anything? I can barely picture it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — a quiet night — what does that bring up for you when you try to picture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Something like... relief, maybe? It almost makes me a little emotional actually, which is weird. Like, it shouldn't be a big deal. But I haven't had that in so long. A night that just felt okay. Not medicated, not numbed — just okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it's important. You came in today skeptical — and honestly, with good reason based on your past experiences. You're not someone who avoids the hard stuff; you've been carrying depression for over a decade, you've tried medications, you've tried therapy. And underneath all of that, there's something in you that still wants a different kind of life. Wants a quiet night. Wants to not be here at fifty doing the same thing. That's not nothing. That's actually a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... I don't know. I feel like maybe I've been harder on myself than I needed to be. Like I've been thinking of myself as someone who can't get it together, but maybe — maybe I've just been surviving with what I had.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Surviving with what you had. I think that's exactly right. And now maybe we can start to look at what else might be available to you — not to take anything away, but to give you more options. As a first step, I'm just curious: what would feel manageable to you between now and when we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I could try just noticing. Like when I reach for a beer, actually stop for a second and notice what's going on. I'm not saying I won't do it. But maybe just — pay attention. I think I can do that.
